args.text:
What's gotta happen before ya fire up the Car?

You'll like this one, it's straight outta the old Ford book. Before you even think about startin' the car, fill the radiator (whip the cap off the top) with clean fresh water. If ya can't lay your hands on water that's perfectly clean, strain it through muslin or a bit of cloth like it, so no muck gets in and chokes the little tubes of the radiator. The whole system takes about three gallons (call it 11 litres). Now this is important: don't run the car under its own steam unless the water circulatin' system's been filled. Keep pourin' till you're dead certain both the radiator and the cylinder water jackets are chockers. You'll know the whole water system's full proper when it starts dribblin' out the overflow pipe onto the ground. For the first few days you're drivin' your brand-spankin'-new car, it pays to keep checkin' the radiator and make sure it stays topped up. Top up the water as often as it wants it. Soft rainwater, if you can get it clean outta the tank, beats hard water hands down, cos hard water can carry alkalies and other salts that tend to leave sediment behind and clog up your radiator. (See chapter on Cooling System.)

What about the Petrol?

The ten-gallon (about 38-litre) petrol tank wants fillin' (nearly to the brim), and never let it get low. Now listen, cos this bit's serious: when you're fillin' the tank, make bloody sure there's no naked flames within several feet, cos that vapour is dead volatile and it gets around quick smart. And always be careful strikin' a match anywhere near where petrol's been spilt, cos the air for several feet round about is thick with the highly explosive vapour. Don't let the little vent hole in the petrol tank cap get bunged up, either, or the petrol won't flow proper to the carburettor. If you need to drain the petrol tank, just open the pet cock in the sediment bulb at the bottom.

What about the Oilin' System?

Soon as the car's yours, see that a good slug of medium light, top-shelf petrol engine oil gets poured into the crank case through the breather pipe at the front of the engine (there's a metal cap sittin' on it). Get down under the car to the flywheel casin' (that's the reservoir that holds the oil) and you'll find two pet cocks. Pour the oil in nice and slow till it runs out the upper cock. Leave that cock open till it stops runnin', then shut it. Once the engine's well and truly limbered up, you'll get the best outta her keepin' the oil halfway between the two cocks, but whatever you do, don't ever let it drop below the lower cock. Every other part of the car's been oiled proper before it leaves the factory. Still, it won't hurt to check all the grease cups are full and that oil's gettin' to the bits that need it. (See Cut No. 18, also chapter on Lubrication.)

How do the Spark and Throttle Levers work?

Under the steerin' wheel you've got two little levers. The right-hand one (the throttle) decides how much mixture (petrol and air) goes into the engine. With the engine goin', the further you pull this lever down toward yourself in the driver's seat (that's called "opening the throttle"), the faster she runs and the more grunt she gives ya. The left-hand lever looks after the spark, which is what sets off the gas in the engine's cylinders. Shove this lever along and you "advance the spark," and you wanna ease it down notch by notch till the motor seems to hit her top speed. Push the lever past that point and you'll hear a dull knock in the engine, which is her tellin' ya you've gone too far. (See chapter on Ignition.)

Where do these levers go when ya start the Engine?

The spark lever usually wants to sit about the third or fourth notch of the quadrant (that's the notched half-circle the levers work on). The throttle usually wants openin' about five or six notches. Give it a few goes and you'll soon have the hang of where these levers go for a proper start. Just be careful not to advance the spark lever too far, cos the engine may "back kick."
